French School Protests Resume on Small Scale After Holiday Break

02 Nov 2026, 06:05 PM IST · GlobeWire Daily World Desk · Source: www.aljazeera.com

2 min read

Key takeawaysHigh school students in France have resumed demonstrations following a two-week holiday break, though participation remains significantly lower than in previous weeks.

Image: Al Jazeera Staff · Photo source · Resized and letterboxed to 16:9; no AI generation

In this article
  1. Current Status of Protests
  2. Background and Student Demands
  3. Government Response and Union Stance
  4. Practical Implications and Verification

High school students in France have resumed demonstrations following a two-week holiday break, though participation remains significantly lower than in previous weeks.

Current Status of Protests

According to data from the Ministry of Education and reports by public broadcaster Franceinfo, approximately 41 high schools—representing about one percent of the country’s 3,700 institutions—were blockaded on Monday. Reuters reported that students attempted blockades in major urban centers including Paris, Marseille, and Rennes, contrasting with the hundreds of schools affected in weeks prior to the break.

Education Minister Edouard Geffray characterized the renewed activity as marginal. Speaking to France Inter radio, Geffray stated that while peaceful protests are permitted, blocking access to educational facilities is illegal. He added that the academic year for hundreds of thousands of students remains at risk and cannot be compromised.

Background and Student Demands

Originating in the Paris suburbs in September, the student-led movement initially focused on educational grievances before expanding last month to broader cost-of-living concerns, which drew participation from trade unionists and activists. Some earlier demonstrations involved clashes with police, property damage, and looting in various cities.

Students have outlined several core demands:

  • Renovation of aging school infrastructure
  • Increased staffing levels and more teachers
  • Expansion of university places
  • Modification or replacement of the current university admissions system, which protesters view as socially unfair

Government Response and Union Stance

In an effort to address the concerns, the government recently announced several measures, as reported by Franceinfo:

  • A gradual replacement of the Parcoursup admissions platform by the year 2028
  • Cancellation of previously planned education job cuts
  • The addition of 500 new posts and a class size cap of 28 pupils for the first year of high school
  • Financial commitments totaling 4 billion euros ($4.47bn) for school renovations
  • The creation of 15,000 new higher education positions

Despite these concessions, student representatives maintained that the government's offers are insufficient. Pierre Sourzat, president of the student organisation Les Lyceens!, confirmed calls for ongoing blockades. Furthermore, the Union Syndicale Lyceenne, Student Union, and UNEF have advocated for additional disruptions, with UNEF designating Tuesday as a national day of action across universities.

Practical Implications and Verification

Commuters and students should check local transit and institutional updates for potential disruptions near affected schools and universities. Independent verification of ongoing demonstrations can be sought through verified local news outlets and official announcements from the French Ministry of Education.
